525:<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The CKgP was introduced in work of Totaro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite> and Bae–Schmitt <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, and plays a key role in the author’s work with Canning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> on the Chow rings of moduli spaces of curves. The following result
567:<p id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> be given. Suppose <math id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g^{\prime},n^{\prime}})=R^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g^{\prime},n^{\prime}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2g^{\prime}+n^{\prime}\leq 2g+n</annotation></semantics></math>. Then <math id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})=R^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})=R^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmthm4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}</annotation></semantics></math> has the CKgP.</span></p>
573:<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text">The boundary of <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}</annotation></semantics></math> is surjected onto by the disjoint union of <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{1},n_{1}+1}\times\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{2},n_{2}+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{1},n_{1}+1}\times\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{2},n_{2}+1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-1,n+2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g-1,n+2}</annotation></semantics></math>. Each of the moduli spaces involved has either genus or number of markings smaller than <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, we can inductively assume that they all have the CKgP and tautological Chow rings. The CKgP implies that the Chow ring of <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{1},n_{1}+1}\times\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{2},n_{2}+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{1},n_{1}+1}\times\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g_{2},n_{2}+1}</annotation></semantics></math> is generated by pullbacks of tautological classes from the two factors. Since the tautological rings are closed under pushforward along gluing maps, it follows that all classes supported on the boundary of <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}</annotation></semantics></math> are tautological, which implies <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})=R^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})=R^{*}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})</annotation></semantics></math>. To see that <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}</annotation></semantics></math> also has the CKgP, we use the fact that the CKgP plays well with stratifications and surjective maps, see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, Lemma 4.1]</cite> for more details.
581:More precisely, in the cases where it has been shown that <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})=R^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})=R^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})</annotation></semantics></math>, it is because the moduli space can be stratified into pieces, each of which is surjected onto by a space whose Chow ring is not hard to calculate, such as an open substack of a Grassmann bundle over <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\BGL_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>BGL</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\BGL_{r}</annotation></semantics></math>. Such tractable spaces tend to have the CKgP. Moreover, the CKgP plays well with stratifications and surjective maps, so an argument that <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})=R^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})=R^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{g,n})</annotation></semantics></math> tends to also show
582:that <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{g,n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{g,n}</annotation></semantics></math> has the CKgP, cf Remark <a href="#S3.Thmthm1" title="Remark 3.1. ‣ 3. When are the Chow or cohomology rings tautological? ‣ Chow rings, cohomology rings, and point counts of moduli spaces of curves" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>. When <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> are large however, the moduli spaces <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{g,n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{g,n}</annotation></semantics></math> are of general type, so in particular do not admit such nice unirational parameterizations. While this means the techniques used for small <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> necessarily break down for large <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmthm5.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>, we do not know of direct arguments in general for the existence of non-tautological classes or failure of CKgP just based on the birational geometry of the moduli space.</p>
595:<p id="S2.Thmthm6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmthm6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">If <math id="S2.Thmthm6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> is a smooth, proper Deligne–Mumford stack over <math id="S2.Thmthm6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ℂ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{C}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmthm6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> has the CKgP, then <math id="S2.Thmthm6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cl" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>cl</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cl</annotation></semantics></math> is an isomorphism.</span></p>

326:<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The Hodge conjecture is known in only a few important cases. First, the conjecture is true for codimension <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=1</annotation></semantics></math>; this is the Lefschetz <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1,1)</annotation></semantics></math>-theorem. Using the hard Lefschetz theorem, it follows that the Hodge conjecture holds when <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dim(X)\leq 3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0em">dim</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dim(X)\leq 3</annotation></semantics></math>. In particular, the Hodge conjecture holds for <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> whenever the subring <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bigoplus_{k}\big(H^{2k}(X)\cap H^{k,k}(X)\big)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>⨁</mo><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo lspace="0em" maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∩</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bigoplus_{k}\big(H^{2k}(X)\cap H^{k,k}(X)\big)</annotation></semantics></math> is generated by <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{2}(X)\cap H^{1,1}(X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∩</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{2}(X)\cap H^{1,1}(X)</annotation></semantics></math>. In particular, this is true for very general abelian varieties in each dimension <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mat58</a>]</cite>. 595:<p id="S3.p14.1" class="ltx_p">To get strong new results from this formalism, one also needs new ways of establishing the base cases needed to run the inductive arguments in this framework. In <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx19" title="" class="ltx_ref">CLP24</a>]</cite>, this is done using explicit low-genus calculations and algebraicity results for pure weight cohomology, via the Chow–Künneth generation property. The Chow–Künneth generation property is established geometrically, on a case-by-case basis. For instance, for certain moduli of genus <math id="S3.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7</annotation></semantics></math> curves, the key geometric input comes from Mukai’s description of canonical curves as linear sections of an orthogonal Grassmannian. With this framework in mind, the proof of Theorem A is essentially an accounting of the base cases that are currently accessible.</p>

Introduction ‣ On the Hodge and Tate conjectures for moduli spaces of curves" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> relies most heavily on new arguments to establish the base cases for relatively small values of <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> needed to run the induction. This includes point counting arguments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx9" title="" class="ltx_ref">BFP24</a>]</cite>, using the Behrend–Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula for stacks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beh93</a>]</cite>, and applications of the Chow–Künneth generation property <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx17" title="" class="ltx_ref">CL24</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx19" title="" class="ltx_ref">CLP24</a>]</cite>, together with explicit classical constructions of small genus moduli spaces and their Brill–Noether–Petri strata.</span></p>
752:<p id="S4.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The topological prediction that <math id="S4.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})=0</annotation></semantics></math> for odd <math id="S4.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k<11" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo><</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k<11</annotation></semantics></math> is proved in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx9" title="" class="ltx_ref">BFP24</a>]</cite>. At present, all of the known proofs use algebraic geometry in an essential way. In particular, the proofs follow the inductive method of Arbarello and Cornalba <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx1" title="" class="ltx_ref">AC98</a>]</cite>, which relies on mixed Hodge theory and the yoga of weights. 485:<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The Hodge conjecture is known in only a few important cases. First, the conjecture is true for codimension <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=1</annotation></semantics></math>; this is the Lefschetz <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1,1)</annotation></semantics></math>-theorem. Using the hard Lefschetz theorem, it follows that the Hodge conjecture holds when <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dim(X)\leq 3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0em">dim</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dim(X)\leq 3</annotation></semantics></math>. Also, by intersection theory, the image of <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bigoplus_{k}\operatorname{cyc}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>⨁</mo><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mi>cyc</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bigoplus_{k}\operatorname{cyc}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> is a subring of <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{*}(X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{*}(X)</annotation></semantics></math>. In particular, the Hodge conjecture holds for <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> whenever the subring <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bigoplus_{k}\big(H^{2k}(X)\cap H^{k,k}(X)\big)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>⨁</mo><mi>k</mi></msub><mrow><mo lspace="0em" maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∩</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bigoplus_{k}\big(H^{2k}(X)\cap H^{k,k}(X)\big)</annotation></semantics></math> is generated by <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{2}(X)\cap H^{1,1}(X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∩</mo><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{2}(X)\cap H^{1,1}(X)</annotation></semantics></math>. In particular, this is true for very general abelian varieties in each dimension <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mat58</a>]</cite>. The Hodge conjecture also holds when <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> is cellular (i.e. paved by locally closed subvarieties isomorphic to affine spaces), a class that includes Grassmannians, flag varieties, and smooth projective toric varieties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ful98</a>, Example 19.1.11]</cite>, and more generally for smooth and proper linear varieties, in the sense of Totaro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tot14</a>, Theorem 3]</cite>, and for smooth and proper Deligne–Mumford stacks with the Chow–Künneth generation property <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx17" title="" class="ltx_ref">CL24</a>, Lemma 3.11]</cite>. In addition, a recent preprint of Markman proves the Hodge conjecture for abelian varieties of dimension at most 5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mar25</a>]</cite>.</p>
754:<p id="S3.p14.1" class="ltx_p">To get strong new results from this formalism, one also needs new ways of establishing the base cases needed to run the inductive arguments in this framework. In <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx19" title="" class="ltx_ref">CLP24</a>]</cite>, this is done using explicit low-genus calculations and algebraicity results for pure weight cohomology, via the Chow–Künneth generation property. The Chow–Künneth generation property is established geometrically, on a case-by-case basis. For instance, for certain moduli of genus <math id="S3.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7</annotation></semantics></math> curves, the key geometric input comes from Mukai’s description of canonical curves as linear sections of an orthogonal Grassmannian. With this framework in mind, the proof of Theorem A is essentially an accounting of the base cases that are currently accessible.</p>
775:<p id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">We note that the methods of proof for the high degree and low degree results stated here are similar: one rigorously applies the method of Arbarello and Cornalba and establishes as many base cases as possible with current methods. The recent progress required to prove Theorem <a href="#ThmTheorem1" title="Theorem A. ‣ 1.1. Main statements ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ On the Hodge and Tate conjectures for moduli spaces of curves" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> relies most heavily on new arguments to establish the base cases for relatively small values of <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> needed to run the induction. This includes point counting arguments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx9" title="" class="ltx_ref">BFP24</a>]</cite>, using the Behrend–Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula for stacks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beh93</a>]</cite>, and applications of the Chow–Künneth generation property <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx17" title="" class="ltx_ref">CL24</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx19" title="" class="ltx_ref">CLP24</a>]</cite>, together with explicit classical constructions of small genus moduli spaces and their Brill–Noether–Petri strata.</span></p>
911:<p id="S4.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The topological prediction that <math id="S4.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{k}(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n})=0</annotation></semantics></math> for odd <math id="S4.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k<11" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo><</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k<11</annotation></semantics></math> is proved in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx9" title="" class="ltx_ref">BFP24</a>]</cite>. At present, all of the known proofs use algebraic geometry in an essential way. In particular, the proofs follow the inductive method of Arbarello and Cornalba <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx1" title="" class="ltx_ref">AC98</a>]</cite>, which relies on mixed Hodge theory and the yoga of weights. Moreover, the base cases needed to run the induction also seem out of reach by topological methods; they are proved using point counts over finite fields, the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula, and étale-to-singular comparison theorems, as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx9" title="" class="ltx_ref">BFP24</a>]</cite>, or using the Chow–Künneth generation property, as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bibx17" title="" class="ltx_ref">CL24</a>, <a href="#bib.bibx19" title="" class="ltx_ref">CLP24</a>]</cite>.</p>

Put X_{g,n}=M_{g,n}. All cohomology has rational coefficients.

1. Pure-weight finite-generation formula.

For each forgetful map pi_i:X_{g,n}->X_{g,n-1}, define

Phi_{g,n}^k := sum_i pi_i^* W_k H^k(X_{g,n-1})

and define

Psi_{g,n}^k := sum_i psi_i Phi_{g,n}^{k-2}.

For g>=2, there is an isomorphism of pure weight-k Hodge structures

W_k H^k(X_{g,n})/(Phi_{g,n}^k+Psi_{g,n}^k)
  ~= direct_sum_{|lambda|=n} W_k H^{k-n}(M_g;V_lambda) tensor V_{lambda^T}.   (1)

Here V_lambda is the irreducible symplectic local system of weight |lambda| and V_{lambda^T} is the corresponding rational symmetric-group representation.

For completeness, (1) follows as follows. Let pi:C->M_g be the universal closed curve and let f:C^n->M_g be its n-fold fibre product. The open inclusion X_{g,n}->C^n induces a surjection on the lowest weight W_k in degree k: after taking a common smooth normal-crossings compactification, W_k of either smooth open is the image of the compactification cohomology, and the restriction map factors that image. Since f is smooth and proper, its Leray spectral sequence degenerates at E_2. Kunneth therefore gives

H^k(C^n)=direct_sum H^p(M_g;R^{i_1}pi_*Q tensor ... tensor R^{i_n}pi_*Q),

where p+i_1+...+i_n=k and each i_s belongs to {0,1,2}. Pullbacks from C^{n-1} span precisely the summands having some i_s=0. Modulo those summands, multiplication by psi_s spans the summands having i_s=2, because psi_s restricts to the nonzero canonical class in H^2 of the fibre. Thus the remaining term has i_1=...=i_n=1 and is

H^{k-n}(M_g;(R^1 pi_*Q)^{tensor n}).

The Kunneth component of each diagonal class Delta_{ij}, which restricts to zero on X_{g,n}, inserts the symplectic form into the i-th and j-th tensor positions. Quotienting by these contraction images gives the symplectically traceless decomposition

direct_sum_{|lambda|=n} V_lambda tensor V_{lambda^T}.

All maps are morphisms of mixed Hodge structures. Since V_lambda has weight n, taking weight k gives exactly (1). This independently establishes the specialized input used below.

2. The primitive six-marking quotient vanishes.

Apply (1) with (g,n,k)=(6,6,26). Its right side is

direct_sum_{|lambda|=6} W_26 H^20(M_6;V_lambda) tensor V_{lambda^T}.   (2)

Harer's virtual-cohomological-dimension formula gives vcd(Mod_6)=4*6-5=19. This bound applies to every rational local coefficient module: choose a torsion-free normal finite-index subgroup Gamma of Mod_6. It has cohomological dimension 19, hence H^20(Gamma;V_lambda)=0. The Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence for Gamma normal in Mod_6 has finite quotient; its positive-degree rational cohomology vanishes, so H^20(Mod_6;V_lambda)=H^20(Gamma;V_lambda)^{Mod_6/Gamma}=0. Therefore every summand in (2) is zero, and

W_26 H^26(X_{6,6})=Phi_{6,6}^{26}+Psi_{6,6}^{26}.   (3)

3. The degree-26 pullback part vanishes.

For five ordered markings,

vcd(PMod_{6,5})=4*6-4+5=25.

The same finite-index argument gives H^26(X_{6,5})=0. Consequently

Phi_{6,6}^{26}=sum_i pi_i^*W_26H^26(X_{6,5})=0.   (4)

Combining (3) and (4),

W_26H^26(X_{6,6})=Psi_{6,6}^{26}.   (5)

4. The remaining psi-multiple part has type Q(-13).

The verified CKgP theorem THM-0005 applies to X_{6,5}, because 5=c(6). It gives surjectivity of the cycle-class map onto every lowest-weight group and A^*(X_{6,5})=R^*(X_{6,5}). Hence, in degree 24,

W_24H^24(X_{6,5}) ~= Q(-12)^{direct_sum a}

for some finite a: every generating codimension-12 cycle class has Hodge type (12,12), and every subquotient of their span has the same type. It follows that Phi_{6,6}^{24}, being a sum of pullback images of this group, is a finite direct sum of Q(-12).

Each psi_i is an algebraic codimension-one class of Hodge type Q(-1). Therefore the cup-product maps

Q(-1) tensor Phi_{6,6}^{24} -> W_26H^26(X_{6,6})

have images that are finite direct sums of Q(-13). By definition their sum is Psi_{6,6}^{26}. Equation (5) consequently exhibits W_26H^26(X_{6,6}) as a quotient of a finite direct sum of Q(-13). Since the target is pure of weight 26, equivalently because polarizable pure Hodge structures of fixed weight are semisimple, there is a finite r>=0 such that

W_26H^26(M_{6,6};Q) ~= Q(-13)^{direct_sum r}.   (6)

5. Conversion to the exact Borel-Moore target.

The smooth Deligne-Mumford stack M_{6,6} has complex dimension

d=3*6-3+6=21.

Poincare duality for smooth finite-type Deligne-Mumford stacks gives an isomorphism of mixed Hodge structures

W_{-16}H^{BM}_{16}(M_{6,6};Q)
  ~= W_26H^26(M_{6,6};Q)(21).

Using (6) and Q(-13)(21)=Q(8), this becomes

W_{-16}H^{BM}_{16}(M_{6,6};Q) ~= Q(8)^{direct_sum r}.

Thus the exact group is a finite direct sum of Q(8), as asserted. The case r=0 is allowed. No non-Tate summand survives.
